standard.title: Formal time units
standard.description: recognise and use the relationship between formal units of time including days, hours, minutes and seconds to estimate and compare the duration of events
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can recognise and read time on an analog clock to the hour, half-hour and quarter-hour (AC9M2M04). They have not yet worked with the full hierarchy of time units (days, hours, minutes, seconds) or used these relationships to estimate and compare durations.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students recognise the relationships between days, hours, minutes and seconds, and use these to estimate and compare the duration of events.

nodes.label: Relationships between time units
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can state the relationships between days, hours, minutes and seconds and use these to convert between adjacent units.
nodes.minimum_width: State the number of hours in a day, minutes in an hour, and seconds in a minute; convert two given time quantities (e.g. '3 hours = ? minutes').
nodes.typical_width: Apply the full hierarchy of time unit relationships; convert across adjacent units in both directions; explain why the relationships have the values they do (history of 60-based time).
wider: Explore why different cultures have used different time unit systems — e.g. ancient Egyptian hours, Indigenous seasonal calendars
Investigate how digital devices represent time and compare digital time displays with the unit relationships

response_modes.reason: Time unit relationships (60 seconds, 60 minutes, 24 hours) are non-decimal and must be memorised. Practice with varied conversion problems is more effective than broadening context here.

nodes.hinge_reason: Time unit relationships are the prerequisite for Node 2 duration estimation and comparison — students who do not know that 1 hour = 60 minutes cannot estimate whether an event will take 'about 45 minutes' or convert between units when comparing durations. The non-decimal relationships are error-prone and must be secure before application.
success_criteria: Students can state the number of seconds in a minute, minutes in an hour, and hours in a day.
Students can convert a given duration between adjacent time units.

nodes.label: Estimating and comparing durations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can estimate the duration of familiar events in appropriate units and compare durations using the time unit relationships.
nodes.minimum_width: Estimate the duration of three everyday events in appropriate units and justify the unit choice; compare two durations expressed in different units.
nodes.typical_width: Estimate and measure durations of a range of events; compare using time unit relationships; connect to planning contexts (e.g. planning a party schedule).
wider: Design a daily timetable or sequence of events, applying duration estimation and addition with time units
Investigate how estimating time relates to First Nations Australian seasonal calendars and duration of events on Country

response_modes.reason: Students who estimate time only in structured classroom contexts (sand timers, countdowns) often cannot apply duration reasoning to open-ended real-world planning. Timetable design and culturally situated time-keeping contexts extend the skill.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Timetable design and cultural time-keeping contexts offer genuine real-world planning richness and connect time measurement to purposeful decision-making.
success_criteria: Students can estimate the duration of a familiar event in an appropriate unit and explain the choice.
Students can compare two durations and state which is longer, converting to a common unit if needed.
